These algorithms vary in complexity, explainability, and computational speed. A subset consisted of relatively simple and explainable algorithms, namely Linear regression (LR), Huber regression, LASSO regression, and Ridge regression. Huber regression, as explained before, is robust against outliers. LASSO and Ridge utilize L1 and L2 regularization to improve generalization and reduce overfitting. Additionally, a group of slightly more complex Integration of Data Driven Process Control for Maximizing Energy and Resource Efficiency in WRRFs 39 algorithms were employed including K-nearest neighbors (KNN) and Decision Tree. KNN is simple and intuitive, and works by finding the majority class among the nearest neighbors. However, it can be computationally expensive as it requires storing the entire training dataset and calculating distances for each prediction. Decision Tree is a highly interpretable algorithm that splits data into branches based on feature values. While easy to understand and visualize, decision trees can easily overfit, capturing noise in the training data, which is why different ensemble algorithms were also evaluated. Furthermore, ensemble algorithms tested included Adaptive boosting (AdaBoost), Extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost), and random forest (RF). AdaBoost is a boosting algorithm that combines the predictions of multiple weak learners (typically decision trees) to form a strong predictor. It adjusts the weights of misclassified instances to focus on hard-to-classify examples, improving accuracy but at the cost of increased computational complexity. XGBoost is an advanced implementation of gradient boosting. It optimizes both computational speed and model performance. It uses parallel processing and regularization to handle large datasets and reduce overfitting, making it powerful but complex to tune. RF is an ensemble method that creates multiple decision trees and merges their predictions to improve accuracy and control overfitting. While more robust than a single decision tree, it loses some interpretability due to the ensemble nature. Finally, a more complex and less interpretable algorithm was used which is a support vector machine (SVM) with radial function basis (rbf) kernel. SVM works by finding the optimal hyperplane that minimizes the error, and the rbf kernel allows it to handle complex, non-linear relationships by mapping input features into a higher-dimensional space. It is effective for high-dimensional spaces, but it can be computationally intensive, especially with large datasets. A preliminary space of hyperparameters was defined and Grid search optimization with 5-fold cross-validation was performed to evaluate different algorithms. These models are trained to predict ESS based on the pre-selected high-frequency features. The models’ goodness of fit was evaluated with root mean squared error (RMSE) and R2, as shown in Figure 5-6. Also, the extent of overfitting is considered which was determined based on the percent increase in training R2 in comparison with testing. It can be seen that all simple and interpretable models including LR, Huber, LASSO, and Ridge are underfitting.
